extracted.intended_audience: readers of the New York Tribune; general public, lawmakers, and moral/philosophical readers interested in marriage and divorce policy
extracted.subtask_description: A published sequence of letters and rejoinders debating the moral, religious, historical, and legal standards that should define marriage and justify divorce, and the proper scope of legal remedies (divorce vs. separation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionary definition: marriage as union for life
rubrics_metrics.description: "Marriage: The act of uniting a man and woman for life; wedlock; the legal union of a man and woman for life. Marriage is a contract both civil and religious, by which the parties engage to live together in mutual affection and fidelity till death shall separate them." (Dr. Webster / Worcester definitions quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to ground the claim that 'marriage' properly denotes a life-long, solemn covenant; anything permitting termination before death is, by this definition, a substitute and should not be called 'marriage'. The editorial argues dictionary meaning supports legal and religious permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indissolubility except for adultery (Christ's teaching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cites Matthew xix.9 and the view that 'a marriage can be rightfully dissolved because of adultery alone.' The position: Jesus expressly declared adultery the only valid reason for dissolving a marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an authoritative religious standard: marriage should be indissoluble except where the essential condition (fidelity) is destroyed by adultery. Invoked to argue against broader grounds for divorce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation from bed and board as remedy (not divorce)
rubrics_metrics.description: For cases of brutality and danger ('a pure and gentle woman exposed to the brutalities and cruelties of a beastly sot of a husband'), the law should grant 'a separation from bed and board' rather than dissolution of the marriage tie with liberty to remarry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions this legal separation as the just remedy for abuse—protects the victim yet preserves the marriage bond and prevents freeing the abusive party to remarry. Also used to argue against treating separations as equivalent to divorce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-experiment unions must be named and distinct from marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who 'have devised something better than old-fashioned Marriage' should 'clearly, specifically, set forth its nature and conditions, and should call it by its distinctive name' rather than appropriating the term 'marriage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guideline for legal/social policy: experimental or trial unions (e.g., probationary marriages, trial cohabitation, free-love arrangements) should not be conflated with traditional marriage; they should be transparent and labelled to avoid deception and social confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical record favors lifelong monogamic marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that mankind has tried all modifications (indissoluble monogamic marriage, polygamy, concubinage, easy divorce, free love) and history establishes the superiority of one man to one woman for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of historical experience as an evaluative standard: long-term social outcomes are invoked to justify preserving permanent monogamous marriage and resisting experimental reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divorce law may properly vary with stages of civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that 'there is no absolute right or wrong about this matter of divorce; but that it may properly vary in its details at different stages of civilization.' Moses' divorce law reflected social conditions; modern societies may adapt rules accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal realism: grounds and procedures for divorce are not universally fixed but can legitimately change according to social development and moral progress. This counsels flexibility in legislating divorce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of marriage includes state/community interest in children
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage 'concerns not only the men and women who contract it, but the State, the community, mankind' because its object includes 'the due sustenance, nurture, and education of their children' and parents must discharge obligations conjointly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifies restrictive divorce policy on public-interest grounds: protecting children's welfare and social stability can warrant limiting dissolution of marriages until parental duties are satisfied (e.g., until youngest child attains maturity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness to marry: must know and be one in spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: No couple can innocently take upon themselves the obligations of Marriage until they know that they are one in spirit and so must remain forever; if they rashly enter marriage, the penalty is theirs alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive criterion for individuals and possibly for law: marriage should be entered only by those able to make a life-long commitment; this is offered as a moral standard to reduce unhappy or dissoluble marriages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation (quasi-divorce) tends to immorality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that 'of all the various kinds of divorce... separation from bed and board... has been found, in practice, to be the most immoral in its tendency' because subjects occupy a 'nondescript state' exposing them to temptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy caution: legal separations can have perverse consequences by creating an ambiguous status between married and single, potentially increasing immorality; used to argue against widespread use of such separations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adultery of the heart (thought) as the proper cause for divorce
rubrics_metrics.description: Jesus' teaching that 'Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart' leads to the inference that the proper cause for divorce is not merely the physical act but 'adultery of the heart which quenches conjugal love.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stricter, inner-standard interpretation: grounds for dissolution should consider inner moral failure that destroys conjugal love, not only outward acts; used to argue for moral seriousness of the marriage bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious vows and conscience can supersede civil law
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that people married by Christian ministers 'solemnly covenanted to remain faithful until death' and that 'a higher law' of conscience may lead them to ignore permissive state divorce laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for evaluation of law and practice: civil permissiveness does not necessarily alter religiously grounded obligations; legislators should consider conscience and religious practice when reforming laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual/legal accuracy matters in arguments about grounds (interpretation of 'uncleanness')
rubrics_metrics.description: Contested interpretation of Deuteronomy xxiv.1 — whether the Hebrew term rendered 'uncleanness' means 'adultery' — with the implication that precise textual reading affects whether Moses' law equated to adultery-only divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological rubric for legal/theological argument: careful, accurate quotation and informed interpretation of scripture/legal texts are essential because small textual differences materially affect legal-moral conclusions about permissible grounds for divorce.
